alinti: How do we make environments like this for our game, despite both being terrible at 3D modeling?
The secret is a technique called projection.
Our artist starts by drawing every asset on an isometric grid that matches the camera angle in our game.
We then project those drawings onto simple 3D meshes.
Once everything's laid out in the level, we add a few extra layers to bring the environment to life.
We add decals to break up the walls and floors and stop the environment from feeling too repetitive.
For light sources, we use hand-drawn animated flipbooks to keep them consistent with the illustrated style.
Then we use lighting and post-processing to create depth and really sell the illusion that everything's 3D.
This process lets us build stylized environments surprisingly quickly, even though we're only a team of two and neither of us knows how to properly model anything.

alinti: Stop losing your important medical paperwork in a messy drawer.
We've all dealt with that frustration of hunting for an old prescription or a blood test result right when we really need it.
This app, called Cura, acts like a digital filing cabinet for your health records that lives right on your phone.
You just snap a photo of any bill, lab report, or doctor's note, and the app reads the information, organizes everything by date, and even flags if your results are high or low.
It's basically like having a personal assistant who remembers every single doctor visit for you, so you can stop guessing about your history or digging through stacks of paper.
The best part is that it's completely private, because it does all the work directly on your device, without sending your sensitive data to some random server.
If you want, it can even help answer questions about your records, but that's totally optional.
It's a clever way to keep your health details clear and searchable without giving up your privacy.
Right now this project has zero stars on GitHub.
Check out the project on GitHub to see how it works.

Örneğin kullanıcı bir ödeme isteği gönderdi. Sunucu isteği aldı. Ödemeyi başarıyla gerçekleştirdi. Ve cevabı kullanıcıya göndermeye çalıştı. Ancak tam o sırada daha da bir problem yaşandı. Ve uygulama bu cevabı alamadı.
Uygulamanın gördüğü şey şu: Ödeme isteğini gönderdim ancak cevap gelmedi. Kullanıcı burada işlemin başarısız olduğunu düşünüp aynı isteği tekrar gönderebilir.
İlk istek aslında sunucu tarafında başarılı tamamlanmıştı. Eğer sunucu gelen ikinci isteği tamamen yeni bir ödeme olarak değerlendirirse kullanıcıdan aynı tutar bir kez daha çekilebilir.
İdempotency'nin amacı aynı isteğin birden fazla kez gelmesi durumunda aynı işlemin tekrar gelmesi ve tekrar tekrar uygulanmasını engellemekte.
Bunun için örneğin her ödeme isteği ile birlikte benzersiz bir Idempotency key gönderilebilir.
Sunucu bu anahtarı kontrol eder. Eğer bu anahtarı ilk kez görüyorsa ödemeyi gerçekleştirir ve oluşan sonucu bu anahtarla ilişkilendirerek kaydeder.
Ancak aynı Idempotency key ile ikinci bir istek gelirse ödemeyi tekrar yapmak yerine daha önce kaydettiği sonucu döndürür.

It acts like a strict security guard that sits between your computer and any AI agent you decide to run. Instead of letting an agent poke around your private files or copy your passwords, you set up a clear list of rules that it has to follow.
If the agent tries to peek at a folder you didn't approve or send data to a website you don't trust, OpenShell just stops it in its tracks.
It even checks its own work to make sure your security rules aren't missing any hidden loopholes before they start.
It's basically a locked room for your agents. It uses AI to do its work without being able to reach anything you want kept private.

How do Chinese AI companies copy Anthropic models? Anthropic just released a full report explaining how. It says Alibaba collected over 151 million exchanges with Claude in three months to train their Quen models.
The technique is called distillation. You take a stronger model, called the teacher, collect its answers, check their quality, and use them to train your own model, called the student.
Training changes the model's weights, the billions of numbers the model calculates with. First, the model cuts your text into tokens, small pieces of words, and turns each one into a list of numbers.
Then, layer after layer, it multiplies those numbers by its weights. Along the way, it looks back at the earlier words, so it understands each word in context.
During training, the teacher's answer tells the student which token should come next. If the student gives it a low probability, training calculates how to adjust its weights to fix that mistake.
Repeat that millions of times, and the student starts answering like the teacher, without ever contacting it.
But here's the catch. All the numbers in between, called hidden states, stay inside Claude. And Claude only shows the token it picked, not its full probabilities.
So the student only learns from the final text, not from how the teacher got there.
That's why Alibaba went after Claude's thinking, the step-by-step reasoning it writes before answering.
It's the closest thing to seeing how it thinks.
A smaller student also can't hold every skill, and it can learn the examples too closely, then struggle with problems it has never seen. That's called overfitting.
So collecting answers can transfer useful skills. The test is whether your model can solve problems it hasn't seen.

alinti: Never, ever, ever use Cloud Code until you install these five plugins.
Number one is Playwright.
Cloud can't see your screen, so it guesses. This plugin gives it eyes and hands so that it clicks, tests, and fixes its own work.
Number two is OmniRoute.
Hit your usage limit and you're dead in the water. This switches you to another model mid-task so that your session never stops.
Number three is Headroom.

Every time you start a new Cloud Code session, it reads everything you've fed, junk included, and you pay for all of it. So what this does is it strips out the noise first, so you get the same output in a much smaller build.
Number four is Mempalus.
Every new chat you re-explain your business from scratch. This gives Claude permanent memory of your projects.
Number five, and this is the one we install on every client project, Frontend Design.
Everything that AI builds sort of looks like AI built it. And this makes your pages look like you hired a real designer.

alinti: This GitHub repo just hit number one trending in the world because it fixes the most expensive and unproductive habit in all of AI, vibe coding.
Vibe coding is a complete waste of your time.
Instead, you should be using the skills in this repo to do something called agentic engineering.
Vibe coding is just prompting and hoping for the best.
Super quick to get started, but before you know it, you're stuck, things are breaking, you're going in circles, and you have no idea how you got there or what to do to fix it.
Agentic engineering, on the other hand, is a more structured process where you remain in control at every step of the process.
You're using AI to plan your work, break it down into smaller chunks, and then you're using agents to test what you've created at each step of the process.
This repo lets you start doing that in five simple steps with a set of skills.
Number one is grill meat. Agents will interview you relentlessly until your plan for what you want to build is absolutely crystal clear.
Number two is specs. The agent turns your conversation into a written spec that outlines exactly what's going to be built in plain English.
Number three is tickets. AI breaks that spec down into smaller chunks with technical instructions that AI can then go and implement.
Number four is build. Each ticket is implemented by a new agent with a fresh context window.
And the fifth and last step is a review. The code is checked. Does it pass all your tests? And does it actually match what you had in the spec at the beginning?

And from there, you remain in control. If you need to iterate, don't go in and blindly change the code. All you need to do is change the spec that's written in plain English and then the agent will change the code for you.
So you remain in control.
Comment 'AGENTIC' below and I'll send you the repo and some tutorials from the creator of this repo, Matt Pocock, who's an absolute legend.

alinti: You can now turn your computer into a tireless research assistant.

alinti: There's a new cloud technique that's been blowing people's minds this week, and it comes straight from the team that built Cloud. It's called a verification loop, and it fixes the most annoying part of using Cloud. You know when you ask Cloud to build something, and it says it's finished, then you try it, and it's actually broken? Basically, a verification loop makes Cloud test its own work before it ever tells you it's done. So instead of babysitting it, Cloud tries out what it built itself.
So if you ask for a new button on your website, it clicks that button itself and actually takes a screenshot to prove it worked.
When something's broken, Cloud fixes it, tests it again, and keeps going until everything actually works.
The first time, Cloud figures out how to test your project and saves those steps so it runs the exact same test every time after.
I put the full setup in a guide comment verified.

alinti: You can now vibe code an entire app without your company's data ever leaving its own cloud. You basically describe the internal tool or the customer portal or the workflow that you want, and Superblocks builds it with AI. But if you already built it in Claude, then you can connect the Superblocks MCP and bring that app straight in to Superblocks. So whether you built it with Superblocks or with Claude, your app can now run in your own cloud with your company's security on it, so your sensitive data stays inside your own infrastructure.

The way that it actually builds is really smart. Most AI builders hand the whole build to one giant agent, but Superblocks splits it across specialized agents. It uses frontier models for the difficult reasoning, and then it hands build work to cheaper open source models running in parallel.

Then, before anything actually ships, security agents check for things like auth bypasses, business logic flaws, and supply chain vulnerabilities, and your existing SSO, permissions, and audit rules can apply automatically across the apps that people are building.

So instead of having to choose between banning Vibe Coding completely or letting everyone build whatever they want with company data, you get a third option. People can build with AI while IT and security still keeps control.

alinti: Everyone talks about Claude, but nobody's talking about effort levels.
And you're probably using the wrong one right now.
Claude Code has 5 effort levels:
LOW: brainstorming, a first sketch, renaming a variable. Anything you’ll read line by line anyway.
MEDIUM: a feature you can describe in one sentence. It’s the default on Opus 5.5, and Anthropic says it matches the old Opus on high.
HIGH: a bug in code that already exists. That’s where the edge cases hide.
EXTRA HIGH: the long stuff, like a refactor or a migration.
MAX: when you’re walking away. ‘Find every security hole in this repo, I’ll be back in an hour.’
Type /effort, pick a level, press S.
And it only lasts this session.
Effort isn’t how smart Claude is. It’s how long Claude is allowed to think before it touches your code.
Save this for the next time you open Claude Code.

Before it keeps an edit, it tests it on tasks it held back on purpose.
Score goes up, the edit is kept. No better, it's thrown out.
And nothing goes live until you type adopt with a backup of the old file.
Okay, how do I get it?

Three steps. One, clone the repo from GitHub. Two, in Claude code, add the plugin from the repo's plugins folder and install SkillOptSleep. Three, type slash SkillOptSleep dry run to preview what it would learn.
Then run, then adopt what you like.

alinti: This GitHub repo is insane if you're looking to repurpose long-form content into short-form clips.
The repo is called ClaudeShorts and it's available on GitHub and it's basically an interactive long-form to short-form video creator.
This is a Claude skill which transcribes the provided video, analyzes the video, and then identifies the best possible snippets that can be turned into short form clips.
It uses re-motion, animated captions, segment scoring, which scores each clip across multiple different categories like the hook strength, the coherence, emotion, value density, and ultimate payoff.
So it's actually using qualitative data to make those short form clip determinations.
It comes with three different caption styles.
It uses cursor tracking to really take care of that issue of converting a long form horizontal video into a short form vertical video and it never cuts things mid-word or mid-sentence.
This repo is crazy powerful if you are a content creator, if you are a marketer and you're looking to repurpose your content to short form media platforms.
So definitely check it out.

alinti: Self-evolving agent harnesses are here 🤖 Today you pick a fixed harness, and every task runs through it. A deep research question and a file-renaming task get the same memory strategy, the same planner, and the same tools exposed at every step. JIT-Agent is a 27B open-source model that writes the harness instead. You hand it the task and the tool registry, and it emits four Python files plus a prompt config before the task starts.
A second model does the actual work by being called step by step from inside those files. It never writes any of the code and never sees it.
Each file covers one part of a fixed four-module contract: ➡️ Memory decides what slice of history the working model sees at the current step ➡️ Planning turns that view into a directive for the next
Overview of JIT-Agent. Given a task, JIT-Agent composes a problem-specific agent harness by selecting and instantiating four modules: memory, planning, action, and capability orchestration.

alinti: JIT-Agent is a compact meta-agent that writes your agent harness on-the-fly. alinti: This AI is finally reading the language of money. It's called Kronos, and it's already gathered 41,391 stars on GitHub because it's the first project built specifically to understand stock market charts.
Think of the stock market like a giant, messy library filled with endless, noisy updates that move way too fast for a human to track.
Kronos acts like a super smart librarian that's been trained on data from over 40 global exchanges to actually make sense of all those shifting price patterns.
It turns complicated financial movements into a simpler code that a computer can read and process, which helps it predict where prices might head next.
This model doesn't just guess blindly. It handles the crazy ups and downs of trading data by breaking them down into smaller pieces that are much easier to manage.
You can use it to forecast how a specific asset might behave over the next day, which gives you a clear picture of potential market trends without getting lost in the noise.
It's a tool that takes the chaotic, fast-paced language of candles and lines and translates it into something much more useful for anyone trying to analyze the financial world.

Supra-Tex can turn a single photograph into a fully textured 3D model, preserving tiny details like lettering and material boundaries. alinti: Game Dev Secret. Why does a boss kill feel so good?
First, mark the bar. A notch at half. Something's coming.
Then, pause it. Can't be hurt.
It cracks open. And the arena breaks.
Save a checkpoint. New moves. A core beam.
Hide behind a rock. And little minions.
Old moves get meaner. Fire left behind.
Throws in threes. And a slam that waits.
At low health, the big one. Hit the core before it blows.
If they die, show how close. Then back to the checkpoint. Not the start.
Secret. Your last bit of health counts double. So you just survive.
Finally, slow it down. Freeze. Flash.
Let it fall apart. Rock by rock. And the core goes out last.
Now that's a boss fight. Save this for your next game.

deger: Post by ohmo.ai OHMO AI NVIDIA open sourced Lyra 2.0, a framework that turns a single image into a 3D world you can walk through. It first generates a long video along a camera path you draw, then rebuilds it as a 3D scene you can explore in a viewer. alinti: Don't start vibe coding with Claude Code until you've installed these five design plugins.

alinti: The seven levels of DevOps. Each one fixes a problem the last one can't.
Level one, Git.
Git saves every change, like checkpoints in a game. So when it breaks, you rewind and see what changed.

Level two, CI/CD. Git saves your code but doesn't check it. So every push now runs your tests automatically. A failing test stops bad code from going live. Code that passes ships on its own. So you can ship small changes every day safely.

Level three, Docker. Your code passed every test on your laptop. Then it crashes on the server. Why? The server has different versions installed. So Docker packs your app with everything it needs. Like a shipping container, it runs the same everywhere.

Level four, Terraform. Now that container needs servers to run on. Most people set them up by clicking around, but nobody remembers the clicks. With Terraform, your whole setup lives in a file. You don't have to run the file. Lose everything, run the file, and it's all back.

Level five, Kubernetes. Your servers are up, but apps still crash. So you tell Kubernetes: keep three copies running. Like a thermostat, it holds that number. One crashes at 3 a.m.? Kubernetes replaces it. Nobody wakes up.

Level six, Metrics. Kubernetes handles crashes, but how do you spot trouble early? With Metrics, numbers your servers report, like CPU. CPU at 70%. Is that bad? You only know by comparing it to normal. Track it constantly, and odd spikes jump out.

Level seven, error budgets. Spikes will still happen. Nothing is up 100%. So you pick a target, like 99.9%. That allows 43 minutes of downtime a month. That's your error budget. Budget left, keep shipping. Budget gone, stop and fix first.

Then just open the prompt window to customize the background. For example, you could place your car on a tropical beach.

Most trading bots are single model wrappers.

This is useful for researchers testing agentic decision pipelines and for teams prototyping AI-assisted trading systems.
The CLI and package layout make it easier to run experiments or integrate the framework into a larger stack.
The readme shows separate analyst and researcher teams.
The readme also documents persistence and recovery.

alinti: Stop writing long prompts. RCCF. 4 lines. 47 words. Better results than a 500-word chain-of-thought prompt.
RCCF is a 4-line prompting method: Role, Context, Constraint, Format.
Role tells Claude who to be (not 'act as an expert' but 'you are a technical writer who hates buzzwords').
Context gives the situation. Constraint sets the guardrails. Format tells how to structure the output.
Claude already knows how to reason. It doesn’t know your specific constraints. RCCF gives it exactly what it needs in 4 lines.
R=Role: Who Claude should be. Gives personality and expertise. Not 'act as an expert.' Specific: 'You are a technical writer who hates buzzwords.'
C=Context: The situation Claude needs to understand. Who’s reading. What they know. What they need.
Example: 'This docs page is for engineers who’ve never used our API.'
C=Constraint: Guardrails and limits. How the output looks.
Example: 'One code example. No exclamation points. Markdown with H2 title. Under 300 words. Bullet points only.'
F=Format: How the output should look.
Example: 'Professional email. Under 150 words.'

THE PROMPT (47 WORDS): ROLE: 'You are a technical writer who hates buzzwords.' CONTEXT: 'This docs page is for engineers who’ve never used our API.' CONSTRAINT: 'One code example. No exclamation points.' FORMAT: 'Markdown with H2 title and bullet points only.'

RCCF for an email: R: 'You are a polite but firm account manager.' C: 'Client wants a refund but is past the 30-day window.' C: 'Offer a credit instead. Don’t apologize excessively.' F: 'Professional email. Under 150 words.'

RCCF for a LinkedIn post: R: 'You are a founder sharing a real lesson.' C: 'I fired my first employee. It was my fault, not theirs.' C: 'No motivational cliches. Raw and honest. Under 200 words.' F: 'Short paragraphs. End with one takeaway.'

RCCF for a strategy doc: R: 'Product strategist at a B2B SaaS company.' C: 'Losing mid-market deals to a cheaper competitor.' C: 'Focus on retention, not acquisition. Use data.' F: 'One-pager. Exec summary, recommendations, next steps.'
Why RCCF works better than long prompts: RCCF tells Claude WHAT matters. Constraints, not steps. Fewer words. Better results.

RCCF template: R-ROLE: You are a [specific role] who [key trait]. C-CONTEXT: This is for [audience] who [situation]. C-CONSTRAINT: [Word limit]. [What to include]. [What to avoid]. F-FORMAT: [File type]. [Structure]. [Style].
4 lines. Every prompt. Works with any task.
Save this. Use it as a template for every prompt.

alinti: GLM-5.2 just dropped open source. 744B parameters, 1M context window, and it goes toe to toe with GPT-5.5 on coding benchmarks. The wild part? You can run it locally with llama.cpp on a Mac Studio. Here’s the full setup. What would you build with a frontier model running on your own hardware?

Before you start, let's talk hardware. The 2-bit quantized version needs about 245GB of total memory. That means a 256GB Mac Studio, a 4x RTX 3090 rig with 192GB system RAM, or any workstation with 256GB+ of memory.

First, build llama.cpp from source. This is the engine that actually runs the model on your hardware. Clone the repo, compile with CUDA if you have an NVIDIA GPU, or leave it off for CPU and Apple Metal.
Now grab the actual model weights. Install the Hugging Face CLI and download the 2-bit dynamic quant from Unsloth. This compresses the full 1.51TB model down to 239GB while keeping 82% accuracy.
Point llama.cpp at the downloaded model and run it. Set temperature to 1.0 and top-p to 0.95, those are the recommended settings from Z.ai.
Here's where it gets really powerful. Swap llama-cli for llama-server and you get an OpenAI-compatible API running on localhost.
That means you can plug GLM-5.2 into Claude Code, Cursor, Continue, or any tool that talks to the OpenAI API.

deger: vector-search: TurboQuant — Shannon lower bound'a uygun distorsiyonla kod kitapçığı eğitimi olmadan çalışan 'oblivious quantizer'.
alinti: oblivious quantizer that matches the Shannon lower bound on distortion, with no codebook training and no separate train phase.

alinti: 2–4 bit quantization with strong recall

alinti: Search-time filtering with SIMD optimizations

deger: vector-search: Online ingest — Vektörlerin eklenmesi sırasında yeniden indeksleme gerektirmeyen, eğitim aşaması olmayan işlem.
alinti: Online ingest. Add vectors, they're indexed - no train step, no parameter tuning, no rebuilds as the corpus grows.

deger: vector-search: FAISS karşılaştırması — FAISS'e göre ARM ve x86 platformlarında %12-%20 daha hızlı performans.
alinti: Faster than FAISS. Hand-written NEON (ARM) and AVX-512BW (x86) kernels beat FAISS 12-20% on ARM and match or beat it on x86.

deger: vector-search: Selective filtering — Araştırma sırasında ID allowlist'i ile filtreleme ve yalnızca izin verilen setten sonuç alma.
alinti: Filter at search time. Pass an ID allowlist (or a slot bitmask) to search() and always get up to k results from the allowed set - no over-fetching, no recall hit.

alinti: Here's how to write a hook so good, it is scientifically impossible to skip.
This is called the triple hook method.
All right, step one is the context.
So the first line of your hook must establish context on what the video is gonna be about.
You can say it in the audio. Seven figure content toolkit.
Now, step two in the triple hook is where most people mess up.
What you're trying to do is get someone curious in a certain direction.
You wanna make them lean in on the context to actively want to hear more.
You can give some proof or stat validating the incoming claim, reference a specific pain point they have or a benefit they want, or share something interesting, shocking, or unexpected.
So when you read back that first one to two sentences just on its own, is the context immediately clear and is there some curiosity inducement that makes the viewer want to lean in for more?
It's called the context lean.
Step three in the triple hook is really where the money's made.
I call it the contrarian snapback.
To catch a fish, you gotta get the hook in its mouth swimming one way and then yank the line going another direction.
The goal is to say something in the contrarian snapback that pulls the viewer away from the direction they were leaning, essentially snapping them back down another path.

That triple combination of rapidly buying into the context, leaning in based on some curiosity, and then getting snapped back in another direction, is the god tier hook formula that works every single time.
Now, if you wanna learn how to actually do this in practice with examples, I've linked a video where I explain it in more detail.

alinti: Dieses kostenlose KI-Tool verwandelt jede Website in ihre eigene API, selbst wenn sie eigentlich keine hat.
Du musst also nicht mehr für Scraping-Tools oder teure APIs bezahlen, selbst bei geschlossenen Seiten wie LinkedIn, Instagram oder Reddit.
Es heißt Reverse API Engineer und ist ein kostenloses Open Source Tool, das du direkt in deinen Code einbinden kannst.
Gib einfach eine Website an und nenne die gewünschten Daten.
Ein KI-Agent durchsucht die Seite, analysiert alle Anfragen im Hintergrund und erstellt daraus einen sauberen API-Client, mit dem du die Daten jederzeit abrufen kannst.
Da es dieselbe API nutzt, auf der die Website selbst läuft, funktioniert es auch dann noch, wenn sich das gesamte Design der Seite ändert.
Alles weiter findest du unten, schau einfach in einen Gepinnt-Kommentar.
1. You give it a website and a goal (fetch all Apple jobs).
2. A browser visits the site, either driven by you or by an AI agent.
3. Network traffic is captured to a HAR file.
4. Your configured model reads the traffic and writes a working API client in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Java, C#, PHP, Ruby, C, or PowerShell.
No more manually opening DevTools, copying cuRL commands, and aluing to aether a client and from.
Reverse API Engineer: Turn websites into APIs. Browse (or let an agent browse), and get a clean, typed client for the endpoints the site actually uses.
